>  **Comment 2.** It will be better if other aspects of conversation quality of the framework such as helpfulness and informativeness, other than the ranking accuracy, can be evaluated.

**Response.** Thank you for your insightful comments. We fully agree that helpfulness and informativeness are crucial for conversational recommendation. For generative ranking tasks such as conversational recommender systems, **catalog-based ranking metrics (Recall@k / NDCG@k)** are the established evaluation criteria and are closely connected tied to perceived helpfulness and informativeness from the users: if the model ranks relevant items near the top of the list and stays in-catalog with the correct format, the user gets more useful and informed recommendations in the conversation. 

>  **Comment 3.** Some claims can be more rigorous. For example, authors claim GRPO is fundamentally misaligned with tasks with rank-style outputs, but the proposed method is still a simple extension of GRPO. If GRPO is fundamentally misaligned, the proposed framework might be something very different from GRPO.


**Response.** Thank you for the insightful comment. By “fundamental misalignment” of GRPO **to rank-style outputs**, we mean that if we use standard GRPO to update policy for rank-style outputs, a **single sequence-level return** is **broadcast to all tokens** in the sequence, leading to unfaithful credit assignment (i.e., token-level policy updates driven by a sequence-level reward; see Eq. (5)). For example, tokens in the weak tail items receive the same positive advantage as those that in the strong head items.

In contrast, Rank-GRPO fundamentally **align the granularity of credit assignment and updates** for LLMs with rank-style outputs. Specifically, we introduce a **rank-wise advantage** and a **rank-wise policy update based on the geometric mean of per-rank importance ratios**, so that both the advantage and the policy update are aligned at the rank level rather than at the sequence level (too coarse) or purely token level (too fine-grained; see Eq. (7)). This is what we mean by “realigning” the objective to rank-style outputs. Empirically, Rank-GRPO consistently outperforms vanilla GRPO/GSPO and RL-free DPO/S-DPO variants on our ranked-list generation tasks, supporting that this design is both necessary and effective in the rank-style setting.

comment.value:
**Hi reviewer 1bEF**, 

Thank you very much for the quick acknowledgement. We really appreciate your insightful feedback to make our paper stronger! We do want to emphasize that Rank-GRPO is more than “just applying a simple extension GRPO to conversational recommendation.” **On the theory side**, our concrete contribution is to show that for rank-style outputs, standard GRPO/GSPO provably apply token- or sequence-level updates driven by a single sequence-level return, which is misaligned with rank-position-wise rewards (see Eqs. (3, 4, 14, 15)). **In addition**, we show that Rank-GRPO theoretically align the granularity of both credit assignment and policy update by it introduces rank-wise advantages and a rank-wise policy update with a geometric mean importance ratio over ranks (see Eq. (6, 7, 16)). In that sense, it is a *non-trivial new RL objective* within the GRPO family, specifically tailored to ranked-list generation from LLM (to more clearly see the fundamental advancement of Rank-GRPO over GRPO for rank-style task, see Eq. (3) and Eq. (6) for the comparison of the objective, Eq. (4) and Eq. (7) for the comparison of the gradient for policy update, and Eq. (14) and Eq. (16) for the derivation).

On the empirical side, we believe the contribution goes beyond “a simple extension” as well: Rank-GRPO is, to the best of our knowledge, **the first RL objective that tightly coupled with the rank-style task where an LLM directly generates full ranked list**, and it consistently outperforms vanilla GRPO/GSPO and strong RL-free preference-alignment methods (DPO, S-DPO, SPRec), as well as powerful prompting/agent baselines such as CRAG built on GPT-4o/Claude, across multiple backbones and two CRS benchmarks. Since conversational recommendation lies in the core of generative ranking and recommender systems in the GenAI era, **we see the contribution of Rank-GRPO as a combination of (i) a theoretically motivated and robust rank-wise RL objective for LLM alignment, and (ii) clear empirical gains over both RL-based and RL-free alternatives, as a substantive step beyond a simple application of GRPO.**

title.value: Further Clarification on the Novelty of the Method

comment.value:
**Hi Reviewer 1bEF,**

Thank you very much for your follow-up and for openly sharing your remaining concerns about novelty. We especially appreciate you pointing us to _In-context Ranking Preference Optimization_ (IRPO, COLM 2025), and this is a very relevant and interesting line of work. We have included the discussion of this work in Section D.3 when we introducing RL-free DPO-based baselines.

We would, however, like to gently clarify that ***(i)* IRPO an is DPO-style algorithm and is generally regarded as RL-free.**  IRPO is built on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which, although originally motivated from the RLHF objective, is typically viewed as an _RL-free_ method because it reduces to maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) on pair-wise preference data. The original DPO paper explicitly states in its introduction that its main contribution is “a simple **RL-free** algorithm for training language models from preferences.” (see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.18290v2). In contrast, **Rank-GRPO is a  PPO-style RL objective**, where we update the LLM-based generative ranking policy based on user-feedback as verifiable rank-wise reward.
    
In addition, we'd love to kindly point out that  ***(ii)* IRPO assumes an _in-context re-ranking_ setup, where a fixed candidate set is provided in the prompt** (see Appendix A.3 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.15477, e.g., "ground-truth movies, GPT-generated movies, and randomly sampled movies"), and the model learns to rank these candidates in-context (this is where the name "in-context" in IRPO comes from). **However, our setting is fundamentally different: the LLM must directly generate a full ranked list of catalog items without being given an explicit candidate set.** To make this feasible, we introduce the Remap–Reflect–Adjust SFT pipeline to teach the model catalog awareness and valid item-tokenization, and then apply Rank-GRPO to optimize rank-wise rewards over these _generated_ lists. So, while IRPO is “in-context **re**-ranking DPO,”, Rank-GRPO is **fully catalog-level generative ranking with RL**.
    
Finally, boiling down to the method, IRPO extends DPO-style objectives to richer ranking structures (e.g., with Plackett–Luce–style modeling), but the **core remains RL-free MLE on comparison data**. By contrast, our contribution is to show that **standard GRPO/GSPO are theoretically misaligned for rank-style outputs** (sequence-level return broadcast to all tokens), and to propose **Rank-GRPO**, which defines **rank-wise advantages** aligned with rank-position rewards, and uses a **rank-wise policy update based on the geometric mean of per-rank importance ratios**, so both credit assignment and updates are aligned at the rank level.
       
We hope this response further clarifies that our work is not just “another application of GRPO to ranking,”  Thank you again for engaging so thoughtfully with our work and for keeping a slightly positive rating. We really enjoy the discussion with you and genuinely appreciate your careful assessment of our work.

display_title: Official Review of Submission8121 by Reviewer uEVq

summary.value: The paper presents ConvRec-R1, a two-stage framework for training LLM-based conversational recommender systems. It combines a supervised fine-tuning pipeline (Remap-Reflect-Adjust) with a new reinforcement learning method (Rank-GRPO) that optimizes recommendations at the rank level. The authors present experiments on REDDIT-V2 that demonstrate solid improvements over baselines, achieving near-GPT-4 performance with smaller open-source models.

strengths.value:
1) The paper addresses an important and emerging problem i.e aligning LLMs for conversational recommendation, which has practical utility for the industry and is a relevant problem for the community.
2) The authors provide code, data, and detailed implementation notes, making the work easy to reproduce and build upon.
3) The proposed rank-level GRPO is a generally useful method for ranking tasks. It's well motivated, includes gradient analysis, and performs reasonably well in practice.
4) The experimental section is detailed and comprehensive, covering different model scales, baselines, and both SFT and RL stages.

weaknesses.value:
1) The core ideas, namely supervised fine-tuning plus RL alignment, primarily extend existing GRPO and RLHF frameworks, without introducing a fundamentally new paradigm.
2) The approach is tightly focused on conversational recommendation and may not generalize well to broader LLM alignment or other ranking tasks, which could limit the paper's impact.
3) The performance improvement over strong prompting baselines (e.g., CRAG) is modest given the added training complexity, and under off-policy settings the method can perform even worse, suggesting limited robustness and stability.
4) All experiments are conducted on the REDDIT-V2 dataset, leaving open the question of how well the method generalises to other domains or item catalogs.
5) The work lacks online or human evaluation, making it unclear whether the improvements translate to better real-world user experience.

questions.value:
1) The paper only uses the REDDIT-V2 dataset without sufficient justification. For a research paper, relying on a single dataset is insufficient to demonstrate generality. Why weren't other conversational recommendation datasets considered?

2) ConvRec-R1 performs worse than CRAG under off-policy evaluation, despite its more complex training. What causes this drop? reward misalignment, data shift, or instability in Rank-GRPO? A clearer analysis would strengthen the paper's claims.

3) The paper reports results on models only up to 3B parameters. Have the authors tested or considered larger LLMs to see whether the proposed Rank-GRPO continues to scale effectively with model size?

**Dear Reviewer uEVq,**

Thank you very much for your constructive feedback. It's our pleasure have this valuable opportunity to discuss with you and address your concerns/questions. We believe that our paper will be much stronger thanks to your efforts.

> **Comment 1.** The core ideas, namely supervised fine-tuning plus RL alignment, primarily extend existing GRPO and RLHF frameworks, without introducing a fundamentally new paradigm.

**Response.** Thank you for your insightful comments. We agree that our work builds on the SFT+RLHF paradigm (as with other many interesting algorithms such as GRPO/GSPO/Dr. GRPO, DAPO, etc.), but we introduce a _new RL objective tailored to LLM-based ranked-style generation_, i.e., Rank-GRPO, which is, to the best of our knowledge, the first RL framework for LLM with rank-style task. The key novelty lies in the use of **rank-wise advantages** together with **rank-wise policy updates based on a geometric mean of rank-level probabilities**, which explicitly aligns each position in the list with its own advantage signal. This differs from GRPO/GSPO, which operate on sequence-level returns with token-level (too fine-grained) or sequence-level (too sparse) policy updates, and from RL-free methods like DPO/S-DPO, which optimize pairwise preferences rather than list-wise rewards.

> **Comment 2.** The approach is tightly focused on conversational recommendation and may not generalize well to broader LLM alignment or other ranking tasks, which could limit the paper's impact.

**Response.** Thank you for your constructive feedback. We intentionally focus our empirical study on conversational recommender system because it sits at the core of GenAI in recommendation research/practice, where _generative ranking / retrieval_ is naturally realized as the model generating a ranked list of catalog-grounded items in dialogue. That said, Rank-GRPO itself is not tied to this domain, as if the (i) items to be represented as a short token sequences, and (ii) rank-wise, verifiable rewards over generated lists are available, the same SFT pipeline can be used to teach catalog awareness and preliminary list-wise behavior into the base model, and Rank-GRPO can then be applied to align the generated ranked lists with user preferences.

> **Comment 3.** The performance improvement over strong prompting baselines (e.g., CRAG) is modest given the added training complexity, and under off-policy settings the method can perform even worse, suggesting limited robustness and stability.

**Response.**  Thank you for your insightful observation. First off, we would like to kindly point out that it is might be a little unfair for us to point out only training complexity while ignoring the inference complexity. In practice, CRAG requires **5–7 GPT-4o API calls per conversation**, which can take minutes per recommendation and depends on a large proprietary model (which could be black-box, slow, and costly) plus a non-trivial agent/RAG pipeline. In contrast, once ConvRec-R1 is trained, a small open model can generate the **entire ranked list as recommendation in sub-second with vLLM**, with no external APIs and no heavy orchestration. We believe that showing that a 0.5B–3B open model can match or surpass GPT-4o/Claude-3.7 + CRAG under these conditions is already a meaningful gain, especially given the large gap in inference latency and deployment cost.

For the off-policy setting, our goal is to **show the efficiency–performance trade-off**, not to claim that off-policy is a better strategy compared to on-policy. Reusing logged trajectories generated from the old policies allows us to reduce the per-epoch runtime to about **2/3 of the on-policy cost**, at the expense of some degradation due to standard off-policy distribution shift, which is common across RL-based alignment methods. Importantly, across both on- and off-policy training, Rank-GRPO consistently outperforms vanilla GRPO and GSPO, indicating that the proposed rank-wise advantage and rank-wise policy update _stabilize training and improve performance_ even under these more challenging off-policy conditions.

> **Comment 5.** The work lacks online or human evaluation, making it unclear whether the improvements translate to better real-world user experience.

**Response.**   Thank you for your insighful feedback. We acknowledge this limitation, but as an academic work without deployment access, we focus on standard offline ranking metrics (Recall@k, NDCG@k) plus catalog-validity metrics (in-catalog ratio, list-length compliance), which are widely used as proxies for user relevance and system reliability and have been the established evaluation procedure for the CRS literacture (see [1-7...]).

> **Comment 6.** ConvRec-R1 performs worse than CRAG under off-policy evaluation, despite its more complex training. What causes this drop? Reward misalignment, data shift, or instability in Rank-GRPO? A clearer analysis would strengthen the paper's claims.


**Response.** Thank you for your constructive feedback. We would first like to clarify that ConvRec-R1 with Rank-GRPO is **not** “more complex,” but rather **more training-efficient** in the RL stage compared to the on-policy counterpart. In our setting (as with most PPO/GRPO-style methods), the dominant cost is generating rollout trajectories: autoregressive generation is expensive and requires many calls to the policy. The off-policy variant allows us to **reuse previously sampled trajectories** and update the policy with importance reweighting, which reduces the per-epoch wall-clock time to about **two-thirds** of the on-policy cost. The downside is stronger distribution shift between the logging policy and the updated policy; correcting this with importance weighting can introduce higher variance, which explains the slight performance drop under purely off-policy evaluation.

In addition, as mentioned earlier, despite the RL training cost, a smaller LLM trained with ConvRec-R1 is substantially more efficient at inference time than CRAG: CRAG typically requires **5–7 GPT-4o API calls per conversation**, whereas ConvRec-R1 produces a full recommendation list in a **single forward pass** of a compact open model (e.g., with vLLM). Thus, even if off-policy performance trades off some accuracy for efficiency, ConvRec-R1 remains far more practical for large-scale deployment than an API-based agent/RAG pipeline.

> **Comment 7.** The paper reports results on models only up to 3B parameters. Have the authors tested or considered larger LLMs to see whether the proposed Rank-GRPO continues to scale effectively with model size?

**Response.**  
Yes. We have added experiments with a **7B backbone** on Redial **(Qwen2.5-7B; see Appendix D.7.2, Table 8)**. Due to computational constraints, we could not run full SFT+RL on the 400k-scale Reddit-v2 dataset with 7B, but we do run the complete ConvRec-R1 pipeline on the Redial dataset, where the results are as follows:

|  + SFT + Vanilla GRPO | 0.2286 | 0.3288 | 0.3753 | 0.4207 | 0.1516 | 0.1879 | 0.2019 | 0.2095 |

**Hi Reviewer uEVq,**

Thank you very much for your follow-up and for increasing your score based on our additional experiments and clarifications. We really appreciate your openness and fairness in reassessing the paper after the revision. Regarding the remaining concerns on **novelty** and **scope**, we would like to gently clarify two points:

1.  **On Novelty.** Rank-GRPO is, to the best of our knowledge, the first _**RL**_ algorithm that studies **directly generating, catalog-grounded ranked lists** from context. The novelty includes **rank-wise advantages** and a **geometric-mean rank-wise importance ratio in the policy update**, as well as our theoretical gradient analysis. This is a non-trivial extension of sequence-level GRPO/GSPO, and we are grateful that you also noted it as a useful method for ranking tasks—well motivated, with gradient analysis, and reasonably good empirical performance.
    
2.  **On Scope.** We agree with you that generative ranking in CRS is a narrower scope than fully general LLM generation. However, generative ranking in CRS is also an important task that lies at the core of recommender systems in the GenAI era. Since generative ranking in CRS is inherently different from free-form text generation, where the model must  produce **ordered, catalog-valid items** rather than arbitrary sequences,  we indeed introduce task-relevant components in the method, which are not intended for general-purpose generation (i.e., narrow the scope).  **We hope that our work can be evaluated within the scope we aim to study, rather than being penalized for the fact that we do not target all generic LLM tasks/all ranking tasks.**
    
Thank you again for the careful evaluation and for recognizing the improvements in the revised version. We really appreciate your insightful and constructive judgement of our work, and our paper is definitely stronger thanks to your effort!

summary.value: This manuscript introduces ConvRec-R1, a two-stage framework for training LLM-based conversational recommender systems. The first stage uses a novel "Remap-Reflect-Adjust" data distillation pipeline to create a high-quality, catalog-aware dataset for SFT. The second stage introduces Rank-GRPO, a new RL algorithm tailored for ranking tasks. Rank-GRPO reframes the RL update unit to the "rank position" level, addressing fundamental flaws in standard GRPO like non-causal credit assignment. Experiments show the framework improves recommendation quality (Recall and NDCG) and allows smaller open-source LLMs to outperform larger, zero-shot models.

strengths.value:
1.	Rank-GRPO is a main contribution. The manuscript clearly identifies the core weaknesses of applying standard GRPO to ranking tasks and proposes an new solution by re-framing the problem at the rank level. The technical solutions are well-motivated and supported by theoretical analysis.
2.	The "Remap-Reflect-Adjust" pipeline is a significant engineering contribution that provides a sophisticated solution to the critical data scarcity problem in this domain. It is quite practical for researchers and practitioners aiming to deploy LLM-based CRS.
3.	The experimental design is robust. The results clearly show the value of each stage of the framework and validate the superiority of Rank-GRPO over its baselines. The finding that a well-aligned 3B model can outperform a much larger zero-shot model is certainly relevant.

weaknesses.value:
1.	The manuscript utilizes an “LLM as a judge” in its data pipeline but does not adequately discuss or account for known biases of this paradigm, such as position or verbosity bias, which could affect the quality of the SFT dataset.
2.	All experiments are conducted on a single dataset in the movie domain. The manuscript would be stronger with a discussion on the potential challenges of applying the framework to other domains like e-commerce or music.
3.	The manuscript notes that the model's outputs tend to drift out-of-catalog during RL training. This practical limitation deserves more prominent discussion in the main text, including the final out-of-catalog rate and potential mitigation strategies.
4.	The primary results table (Table 1) omits a direct on-policy comparison with GSPO, a relevant and stronger baseline discussed elsewhere in the manuscript. Including this would make the evaluation of Rank-GRPO's advantage more complete.
5.	The multi-step SFT data pipeline involves a lot of components and hyperparameters. The manuscript lacks an analysis of how sensitive the final data quality is to these choices, which would be valuable for reproducibility and practical application.

questions.value:
1. Can you elaborate on measures taken to mitigate potential biases (e.g., position bias) from the LLM-as-a-judge used in the "Reflect" step?
2. What is the final out-of-catalog recommendation rate on the test set, and what are potential strategies to better enforce catalog constraints during the RL phase?
3. Why was the GSPO baseline omitted from the main on-policy results in Table 1, given it is a key point of comparison?
4. How sensitive is the model's performance to the new penalty hyperparameters (ϵ_u, ϵ_o) introduced in Rank-GRPO?

**Dear Reviewer o3UH,**

Thank you very much for your constructive feedback. It's our pleasure have this valuable opportunity to discuss with you and address your concerns/questions. We believe that our paper will be much stronger thanks to your efforts.

> **Comment 1.** The manuscript utilizes an “LLM as a judge” in its data pipeline but does not adequately discuss or account for known biases of this paradigm, such as position or verbosity bias, which could affect the quality of the SFT dataset.

**Response.**  Thank you for your constructive feedback. To establish a high-quality behavior cloning dataset, the LLM-as-a-judge in the **Reflect** step intends to *correct* the ranking bias in the list generated by the previous *Remap* step. Specifically, the *Remap* step builds a catalog-grounded recommendation list from zero-shot recommendation of a teacher model by remapping out-of-catalog title back to in-catalog titles based on **shallow content similarity**, whereas the **Reflect** step uses LLM's knowledge to score each item in the list according to how good the item for the conversation and rerank the items based on the score. This is similar to the reflection step in the CRAG framework \[1\], which finds that an LLM-judge with a pre-defined score space can effectively down-weight (or upweight) context-irrelevant (or relevant) titles even if they appear in front (or end) positions without being influenced by position bias, compared to the case if directly ask the LLM to generate a reranked list. 

In addition, we have added an ablation on the **Reddit-v2** dataset (**see Section 4.3, Table 4 in the revised paper**) where we remove the Reflect step and see how it influences the SFT stage. The results are summarized as follows:

| Method | R@5 | R@10 | R@15 | R@20 | N@5 | N@10 | N@15 | N@20 |

[1] Collaborative Retrieval for Large Language Model-based Conversational Recommender Systems, WWW 2025.

> **Comment 2.** All experiments are conducted on a single dataset in the movie domain. The manuscript would be stronger with a discussion on the potential challenges of applying the framework to other domains like e-commerce or music.

**Response.**   Thank you for your constructive feedback. We have addressed this concern in two ways. First, in the revision, we incorporate a full set of experiments on the Redial dataset  in appendix (**see Section D.7, “Additional Experiments on Redial”, with results illustrated Figures 7,8,9,10 and Tables 5,6,7**). > **Comment 3.** The manuscript notes that the model's outputs tend to drift out-of-catalog during RL training. This practical limitation deserves more prominent discussion in the main text, including the final out-of-catalog rate and potential mitigation strategies.

**Response.**   Thank you for your insightful observation. We fully agree and have added both quantitative results of in catalog rate and a clearer discussion of potential strategy for mitigation. Specifically, on the Reddit-v2 dataset, we summarize the in-catalog ratios ConvRec-R1 after RL stage in both on-policy and off-policy.


For Reddit-v2, we summarize the in-catalog ratios after the RL stage as follows:

| ConvRec-R1 on Reddit-v2          | Qwen2.5-0.5B | Llama-3.2-1B | Llama-3.2-3B |
|----------------------------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| On-policy in-catalog ratio (%)   | 99.61 $\pm$ 1.50 | 98.40 $\pm$ 3.76 | 99.46 $\pm$ 1.77 |
| Off-policy in-catalog ratio (%)  | 98.52 $\pm$ 3.21 | 98.51 $\pm$ 3.31 | 99.50 $\pm$ 1.76 |

For Redial, the corresponding in-catalog ratios after the RL stage as follows:

| ConvRec-R1 on Redial             | Qwen2.5-0.5B | Llama-3.2-1B | Llama-3.2-3B |
|----------------------------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| On-policy in-catalog ratio (%)   | 97.77 $\pm$ 3.71 | 98.12 $\pm$ 3.72 | 98.53 $\pm$ 3.12 |
| Off-policy in-catalog ratio (%)  | 97.93 $\pm$ 3.60 | 95.52 $\pm$ 5.41 | 97.82 $\pm$ 4.30 |


We note that in all settings, after SFT + RL more than 98\% of generated items are in-catalog. Since it is relatively rare to encounter an out-of-catalog title after SFT + RL, a deployed system can further reuse the SFT remapping step to project such outputs onto the nearest valid catalog item, or simply filter them out to effectively eliminating residual out-of-catalog drift in practice.


> **Comment 4.** The primary results table (Table 1) omits a direct on-policy comparison with GSPO, a relevant and stronger baseline discussed elsewhere in the manuscript. Including this would make the evaluation of Rank-GRPO's advantage more complete.

**Response.**  
We apologize for the confusion. The reason we did not include GSPO in the on-policy table is that, under on-policy sampling, GSPO and GRPO reduce to the same policy gradient algorithm. To see this, we first recall the GSPO and GRPO gradients derived in our paper (Eq. (14) and Eq. (15) in the appendix) as follows. Specifically, the GSPO gradient is
$$
\nabla\_\theta \mathcal{J}\_{\text{GSPO}}(\theta)
\propto
\mathbb{E}\_{\pi\_{\theta\_{\text{old}}}}
\Bigg[
\sum\_{i=1}^{G}
s\_i(\theta)\ \cdot \hat{A}\_i\ \cdot
\frac{1}{|y\_i|}
\sum\_{t=1}^{|y\_i|}
\nabla\_\theta \log \pi\_\theta(y\_{i,t} \mid x, y\_{i,<t})
\Bigg].
$$
The GRPO gradient is
$$
\nabla\_\theta \mathcal{J}\_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)
\propto
\mathbb{E}\_{\pi\_{\theta\_{\text{old}}}}
\Bigg[
\sum\_{i=1}^{G}
\frac{1}{|y\_i|}
\sum\_{t=1}^{|y\_i|}
w\_{i,t}(\theta)\cdot\hat{A}\_i\cdot
\nabla\_\theta \log \pi\_\theta(y\_{i,t} \mid x, y\_{i,<t})
\Bigg].
$$

where Let $\(s\_i(\theta)\)$ denote the sequence-level importance ratio and \($w\_{i,t}(\theta)$\) the token-level importance ratio, respectively. In the on-policy setting, we have $\(\pi\_\theta = \pi\_{\theta\_{\text{old}}}\)$, so both importance ratios become 1:

$$s\_i(\theta) =\frac{\pi\_\theta(y\_i \mid x)}{\pi\_{\theta\_{\text{old}}}(y\_i \mid x)}= 1,w\_{i,t}(\theta)
=\frac{\pi\_\theta(y\_{i,t} \mid x, y\_{i,<t})}{\pi\_{\theta\_{\text{old}}}(y\_{i,t} \mid x, y\_{i,<t})}= 1.
$$

Substituting $\(s\_i(\theta) = 1\)$ and $\(w\_{i,t}(\theta) = 1\)$ into the two expressions yields
$$
\nabla\_\theta \mathcal{J}\_{\text{GSPO}}(\theta)
\propto
\mathbb{E}\_{\pi\_\theta}
\Bigg[
\sum\_{i=1}^{G}
\hat{A}\_i\cdot
\frac{1}{|y\_i|}
\sum\_{t=1}^{|y\_i|}
\nabla\_\theta \log \pi\_\theta(y\_{i,t} \mid x, y\_{i,<t})
\Bigg],
$$
$$
\nabla\_\theta \mathcal{J}\_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)
\propto
\mathbb{E}\_{\pi\_\theta}
\Bigg[
\sum\_{i=1}^{G}
\frac{1}{|y\_i|}
\sum\_{t=1}^{|y\_i|}
\hat{A}\_i\cdot
\nabla\_\theta \log \pi\_\theta(y\_{i,t} \mid x, y\_{i,<t})
\Bigg] = \mathbb{E}\_{\pi\_\theta}
\Bigg[
\sum\_{i=1}^{G}
\hat{A}\_i\cdot
\frac{1}{|y\_i|}
\sum\_{t=1}^{|y\_i|}
\nabla\_\theta \log \pi\_\theta(y\_{i,t} \mid x, y\_{i,<t})
\Bigg].
$$
which leads to the **same on-policy policy gradient objective**.

> **Comment 6.** How sensitive is the model's performance to the new penalty hyperparameters ($\epsilon\_u, \epsilon\_o$) introduced in Rank-GRPO?

**Response.**  We appreciate this question and have added a dedicated sensitivity study to the appendix (Appendix D.7.3). In Rank-GRPO, we use $\epsilon\_{o} < 0$ for both per-token penalties for overflow tokens beyond the desired list length $N$ and for premature EOS that stops the list early (sorry for the typo $\epsilon_{u}$). This encourages the model to output exactly $N$ items with the correct format and helps reduce out-of-catalog drift. 

To study sensitivity, we consider $\epsilon\_o \in [0.00, -0.01, -0.10, -0.50, -1.0]$ for the Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone on Reddit-v2 under Rank-GRPO ($\exp_{\infty}$) and track Recall@20. Specifically the results are summarized as follows: (see Appendix D.7.3, Figure 10):

| $\epsilon\_{o} $ | 0.00 | −0.01 | −0.10 | −0.50 | −1.00 |
|--------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| Recall@20 | 0.4284 | 0.4444 | 0.4410 | 0.4443 | 0.4435 |

Qualitatively, $\epsilon\_o = 0$ leads to the worst Recall@20 because the model might violate the list-length and format constraints. Once any negative penalty is applied, the failure can be punished, which leads to improved Recall@20 metrics, Further changes in $\epsilon\_o$ within $\left[-1,-0.01\right]$ only have mild effect. This indicates that Rank-GRPO is not very sensitive to the exact penalty values as long as they are negative reasonably.

(6): the mean and std should be taken over the **same rank position $k$ across different responses $i'$**, rather than over different $k'$ within the same response $i$. I apologize for the confusion caused by this typo. I will correct Eq. (6) accordingly after I finish wrapping up the experiments in response to the reviews. Thanks again for catching this and for helping improve the clarity of the paper! I really appreciate it!

summary.value: This manuscript introduces ConvRec-R1, a two-stage framework for training LLM-based conversational recommender systems. The first stage uses a novel "Remap-Reflect-Adjust" data distillation pipeline to create a high-quality, catalog-aware dataset for SFT. The second stage introduces Rank-GRPO, a new RL algorithm tailored for ranking tasks. Rank-GRPO reframes the RL update unit to the "rank position" level, addressing fundamental flaws in standard GRPO like non-causal credit assignment. Experiments show the framework improves recommendation quality (Recall and NDCG) and allows smaller open-source LLMs to outperform larger, zero-shot models.

reviewer_concerns.value:
1, Despite clarifications, derivations, and comparisons (e.g., against DPO, IRPO, GSPO), multiple reviewers still view Rank-GRPO as an incremental extension rather than a paradigm-level contribution.
2, Even with Redial added and discussion of e-commerce/music scenarios, reviewers remain unconvinced that: Rank-GRPO meaningfully generalizes to non-CRS ranking problems, or ConvRec-R1 impacts general LLM alignment or ranking research, beyond this niche. While the authors clearly argue generality, no empirical evidence outside CRS-style conversational datasets is provided.
3, Although ablations show the Reflect step helps, the systemic risks of LLM-judge bias (position bias, verbosity bias, latent preference bias) are not deeply characterized. The rebuttal argues empirical utility, not bias robustness. No explicit bias diagnostics (e.g., controlled position swaps, verbosity-controlled prompts) are presented.
4, No human study, user simulation, or online proxy is added.
5, While ε-penalty sensitivity is shown to be mild, other aspects remain unexplored: Rank-length choice, Reward shaping variants, Reflect prompt sensitivity, Remap similarity thresholds
